# The One Piece of Gear Every New Creator Needs

URL: https://poguedigitalsolutions.com/blog/the-one-piece-of-gear-every-new-creator-needs
Published: 2026-10-08  Updated: 2026-10-08  Topic: Marketing

**The short answer:** Get a selfie stick that also stands up as a tripod, with a small wireless remote. It holds your phone steady, lets you film without anyone else in the room, and folds up small enough to travel. It is inexpensive, and it is the first thing I recommend to every client I coach. The one I suggest is the <a href="https://link.amazon/B0aKdCVgD" target="_blank" rel="sponsored nofollow noopener">Liphisy 50" Selfie Stick Travel Tripod</a>.

*As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. If you buy through a link on this page, I may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you.*

<figure style="margin:28px 0"><img src="/img/selfie-stick-tripod-illustration.svg" alt="Illustration of a phone on a selfie stick tripod, angled down to film hands working on a quilt square, with a small wireless remote on the table" width="800" height="500" style="width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:8px" loading="lazy"></figure>

## Why this comes before everything else

Most of the people I coach are starting a business later in life. They have a smartphone, a story worth telling, and a skill people want to learn. What they do not have yet is a steady way to film it.

Shaky video is the first thing that makes a beginner give up. You prop the phone against a coffee mug, it slides, you start over, and twenty minutes later you have nothing you want to post. A tripod fixes that on day one. The phone stays where you put it, and you get to focus on what you are showing instead of how you are holding the camera.

## What to look for

You do not need anything expensive. You need four things:

- **It stands on its own.** The legs fold out so it works as a tripod on a table or the floor.
- **It extends.** You can raise the phone to eye level or reach over your work for a better angle.
- **It has a wireless remote.** You start and stop recording without walking back to the phone or touching the screen.
- **It folds up small.** You can toss it in a bag and film wherever you are.

The <a href="https://link.amazon/B0aKdCVgD" target="_blank" rel="sponsored nofollow noopener">Liphisy 50" Selfie Stick Travel Tripod</a> checks all four boxes, and it is priced for someone just getting started.

## How my clients use it

**Faceless videos.** Many of my clients would rather not be on camera. That is fine. Set the tripod so the phone looks down at your hands and your work: a quilt coming together, a recipe being made, a tool being used. Your hands tell the story.

**Talking to the camera.** When you are ready to show your face, the tripod holds the phone at eye level so you look like you are talking with a friend across the table.

**On the road.** Visiting family, a trip to a park, a project delivered in person. It packs small, so the content comes with you.

## Your first step

<a href="https://link.amazon/B0aKdCVgD" target="_blank" rel="sponsored nofollow noopener">Order the tripod</a>, take it out of the box, and record one practice video of anything you are working on. Do not post it. Just watch it back and notice how much steadier it looks. That small win is how every channel starts.

If you are one of my coaching clients, bring it to your next session and I will show you how to set it up for the kind of videos you want to make.

# What Should a Small Business Automate First?

URL: https://poguedigitalsolutions.com/blog/what-should-a-small-business-automate-first
Published: 2026-10-05  Updated: 2026-10-05  Topic: AI and Automation

**The short answer:** Automate the task you repeat most often that requires the least judgment. For most small businesses that is one of three things: answering the same inbound question, sending the same follow-up, or moving the same information from one place to another by hand. Pick one. Document how you do it today. Then, and only then, look at tools.

The order matters. Most automation projects fail because they start with software and work backward to a problem.

## Why businesses pick wrong

The usual story goes like this. The owner reads about an AI tool, signs up for a trial, and spends a weekend connecting it to things. By Monday there is a workflow that sends a Slack message when a form is submitted. It is impressive. It also solves nothing, because nobody was losing sleep over form notifications.

Meanwhile, the owner is still personally answering "do you work with businesses my size?" eleven times a week, still typing the same onboarding email with the client's name swapped in, and still copying invoice totals from one app into a spreadsheet every Friday.

The tool got picked before the problem did. That is backward. In the Navy, you diagnose before you treat. Treating symptoms you have not examined wastes supplies and sometimes makes things worse. Automation works the same way.

## Three questions before you automate anything

Here is the diagnosis I run with clients before we talk about a single tool.

**1. What do you do more than five times a week that feels the same every time?**

Write them down. Do not filter. Answering the same email. Scheduling. Chasing a signature. Formatting a report. Posting the same kind of update. Reminding someone of something. You will find more than you expect.

**2. For each one, how much judgment does it take?**

Rate it honestly. Replying to "what are your hours" takes none. Deciding whether a lead is a good fit takes a lot. Drafting a proposal takes some judgment at the start and the end, and almost none in the middle.

**3. What breaks if it is done wrong?**

A late reminder is annoying. A wrong invoice costs money. A tone-deaf reply to an upset customer costs the relationship. The lower the stakes, the better the candidate for early automation.

The first thing to automate is at the intersection: high frequency, low judgment, low stakes. That is where you get the time back fastest with the least risk.

## The one I see most

Across most of the businesses I work with, the winner is the same: inbound questions that already have an answer.

Every business gets the same fifteen questions. Pricing, availability, whether you serve a certain area or customer type, what happens after someone signs up, how to reschedule. The owner answers each one fresh, from memory, slightly differently every time. That inconsistency is its own problem, and it is a brand voice problem as much as an efficiency problem.

Write the fifteen answers once, in your voice. Put them somewhere your team and your tools can read them. Now a form, an email assistant, or a chat tool can give the same correct answer every time, and the owner reviews the ones that fall outside the fifteen. You have not replaced anyone. You have stopped paying a skilled person to retype the same paragraph.

The second most common winner is follow-up. Someone fills out a form, books a call, or buys something, and the next three touchpoints are identical every time. That is a sequence, and a sequence should run itself.

## Automate repetition. Support judgment. Preserve accountability.

That line is the whole philosophy. Automation is for the repeated middle of a process. The decisions at the beginning and the review at the end stay with a person.

A good test: can you write down the exact steps, and would two different people following those steps get the same result? If yes, it is a candidate. If the answer is "well, it depends," you have found a judgment call, and judgment calls get supported with better information, not replaced with a rule.

I keep a human approval checkpoint in every automation I build, even the simple ones. Not because the tools are unreliable, but because a business should always be able to answer "who decided that?" with a name.

## A short story about doing it the hard way

When I migrated 674 files out of three and a half years of ChatGPT history, my first instinct was to find a tool that would sort them for me. I spent an evening evaluating options. None of them knew what my categories should be, because I had not decided yet.

So I did the first fifty by hand. By file thirty I had a pattern: identity, customers, offers, processes, stories, standards. By file fifty I could write the pattern down. Then I handed the remaining 624 files and the written pattern to an AI tool and reviewed its sorting in batches. It took a fraction of the time, and it was right most of the time, because I had done the judgment work first and given it something to follow.

That is the sequence. Do it by hand until you can write it down. Then automate what you wrote down. Keep reviewing.

## What not to automate first

A few things that look like good candidates and are not:

- **Anything customer-facing that touches an upset person.** The cost of getting it wrong is too high to be your first project.
- **Anything you have not done manually at least a dozen times.** You do not understand it well enough yet.
- **Anything you are automating because a tool made it easy.** Easy to build is not the same as worth building.
- **Your content.** AI can draft, but if you automate publishing without review, you will eventually publish something that is not you. Content is a Layer 3 problem; it comes after you have captured your voice.

## An example from a service business

A home services company I worked with wanted to "automate their marketing." That is not a task; it is a wish. When we ran the three questions, the real list looked like this:

- Replying to quote requests with the same four qualifying questions (12 times a week, zero judgment, low stakes)
- Sending appointment reminders (30 a week, zero judgment, medium stakes if missed)
- Writing up the job summary after a visit (8 a week, some judgment, medium stakes)
- Deciding which jobs to bid on (5 a week, high judgment, high stakes)

We automated the first two in an afternoon with tools they already paid for. The third got a template and an AI draft with the tech reviewing it. The fourth stayed with the owner, who now had five more hours a week to think about it.

## Where to start

Take the AI Readiness Assessment if you want a structured read on whether your business has the information, processes, and safeguards to automate well. Or skip straight to the three questions above with a notepad. Either way, you are looking for the task that is boring, frequent, and low risk. That is your first automation, and it is probably not the one the software ad told you about.

# What Is Brand Voice AI?

URL: https://poguedigitalsolutions.com/blog/what-is-brand-voice-ai
Published: 2026-10-05  Updated: 2026-10-05  Topic: Brand Voice

**The short answer:** Brand Voice AI is an AI-assisted business operating system. It captures what a company knows, how it communicates, who it serves, and how it makes decisions, then organizes that into a foundation that people and AI tools can both work from. The result is consistency. Your website, your emails, your proposals, and your AI-drafted content all sound like the same business, and a human approves the work before it goes out.

Most people use AI to make more content. Brand Voice AI uses AI to make the content you already produce more consistent, and to make the knowledge behind it survive.

## The problem it solves

Here is what I see in almost every founder-led business I talk with.

The owner knows the business cold. They know which customers are a good fit and which are a headache. They know why the company does things a certain way. They know the story of how it started, the mistakes that shaped the process, the three questions every new client asks. None of that is written down anywhere useful.

Some of it lives in a branding kit in a Google Drive folder nobody opens. Some of it is in old emails. Some of it is in a notes app. Most of it is in the owner's head, and the owner is too busy running the business to write down how they run the business.

Then AI shows up. The owner opens ChatGPT, types "write me a LinkedIn post about our services," and gets back something that could have been written for any company in any industry. It is grammatical, confident, and completely generic. So they try again with a longer prompt. Better, but still not them. After a week they either give up on AI or start publishing content that sounds like somebody else's company.

The AI did not fail. It was never given anything to work with.

## What Brand Voice AI organizes

Brand Voice AI starts with a structured capture of the business, not a prompt. The categories look like this:

- Mission, vision, and values, in the owner's words
- Founder knowledge and experience: the judgment calls, the hard-won rules
- Brand voice and communication standards: tone, vocabulary, what you never say
- Products, services, and offers, including how you describe them to a stranger
- Customer avatars and audience insights: who you serve and what they are afraid of
- Customer journeys: how someone goes from first hearing of you to referring you
- Stories, examples, and case studies
- Content standards and campaign structures
- Internal processes and playbooks
- Approval requirements: who signs off on what
- AI instructions and safeguards
- The questions customers ask over and over

That list is long on purpose. A brand voice is not a tone setting. It is the sum of what a business knows and believes, expressed in a particular way. Capture only the tone and you get polished writing that says nothing true.

## The three layers

The system is built in three layers, and the order matters.

**Layer 1: Foundation.** This is the capture. I sit with the founder, sometimes for several sessions, and pull out what is in their head one conversation at a time. Identity, audience, offers, stories, differentiators, terminology, tone. It gets written down and organized so a new hire could read it and understand the company.

**Layer 2: Playbooks.** The foundation gets turned into guidance people can follow. How we write a proposal. How we respond to a cold inquiry. What a monthly content cadence looks like. What has to be approved and by whom. This is where the business stops depending on the founder being in the room.

**Layer 3: Execution.** Now the AI tools come in. They read the foundation and the playbooks, and they prepare work in the company's actual voice: drafts, outlines, follow-ups, research summaries. A human reviews and approves before anything is published, sent, or delivered.

The approval step is not optional and it is not a formality. It is the whole point.

## Open big, let AI carry the middle, close big

I describe the working rhythm this way. The human opens big: defines the problem, sets the direction, says what a good result looks like. AI carries the middle: the research, the organizing, the drafting, the repetition. The human closes big: reviews, corrects, adds judgment and experience, puts the story in.

AI can carry the load. It should not choose the destination.

## Where this came from

Brand Voice AI started as a problem I had myself.

In the summer of 2026 I migrated 674 files out of a ChatGPT workspace I had been using for over three years. Marketing plans, customer research, drafts, half-finished frameworks, conversation logs. When I finally saw it all in one place, I realized two things. First, there was a real business in there. Second, almost none of it was organized in a way that another person, or another AI tool, could use.

I spent weeks sorting it into categories. Identity here, customer insights there, processes, standards, stories. When I was done, I could hand the organized set to any AI tool and get back work that sounded like me and reflected what I actually believed. The quality jump was not from a better model. It was from better input.

That is the system I now build for clients.

The other story that shaped it came from a fellow veteran. He had built a solid business over many years and wanted to sell it. Buyers kept walking away with the same objection: "You are the business." Every process, every customer relationship, every bit of judgment lived in his head. The company had no value without him in the chair. He had never written down how he ran it, so there was nothing to sell.

Brand Voice AI is the fix for that problem, whether or not you ever plan to sell. Knowledge that lives only in one person's head is a liability.

## Who it is for

Brand Voice AI fits best for:

- Founder-led companies where the owner's expertise is the product
- Consultants, coaches, and professional service providers
- Solopreneurs preparing to grow or hire
- Businesses whose marketing sounds different depending on who wrote it that week
- Teams adopting AI without any shared standards
- Any organization where too much depends on one person's memory

It is not a good fit for businesses that want AI to run unsupervised, or for anyone looking for a tool that produces volume without a human in the loop.

## A concrete example

A consultant I will call Dana writes a good proposal. It takes her four hours and she dreads it. Her assistant writes a proposal and it comes back wrong in a dozen small ways: the wrong framing of the offer, the wrong tone for that client, a service described in words Dana would never use.

With Brand Voice AI in place, the foundation holds Dana's offer descriptions, her tone rules, her three standard proposal structures, and examples of proposals that won. The playbook says which structure to use for which client type and what Dana must personally review. The assistant, or an AI assistant, drafts a proposal from that foundation in twenty minutes. Dana reviews it in fifteen, changes two paragraphs, and sends it. The proposal sounds like Dana because it was built from Dana.

## Where to start

If you want to know whether your business has enough clarity and documentation to communicate consistently, take the Brand Voice Quick Check. It takes five minutes and ends with a plain read on where you stand. If you already know the knowledge is trapped and you want to get it out, book a strategy call and we will talk about what a foundation session would look like for your business.

Either way, start by asking one question: if I disappeared for a month, what would my business forget?

# How Do You Capture the Knowledge Inside a Founder's Head?

URL: https://poguedigitalsolutions.com/blog/how-do-you-capture-the-knowledge-inside-a-founders-head
Published: 2026-10-05  Updated: 2026-10-05  Topic: Business Systems

**The short answer:** You do it through structured conversation, not a questionnaire, and you do it in rounds. A founder cannot sit down and write out everything they know, because most of what they know does not feel like knowledge to them. It feels like common sense. The job is to ask the questions that make the invisible visible, record the answers, organize them into categories a stranger could use, and then come back for a second pass once the founder sees what they missed.

It is slower than a brain dump and it is the only method I have seen work.

## Why the brain dump fails

Every founder has tried it. Block off a Saturday, open a blank document titled "How We Do Things," and start typing. By noon there are four pages. By the following week the document is forgotten, and six months later it is wrong.

The problem is not discipline. The problem is that expertise hides from the person who has it.

A founder who has handled a thousand customer calls does not experience that as a thousand data points. They experience it as instinct. Ask them how they qualify a lead and they say "I just know." Ask them why they never take projects under a certain size and they say "those never work out." Both answers are true and neither one is usable by anyone else.

When I was a Hospital Corpsman, the Navy taught with one rule: see one, do one, teach one. The teaching step is there because you do not actually understand a procedure until you have to explain it to someone who has never done it. The founder's knowledge works the same way. It only becomes transferable when someone makes them explain it.

## The method: interviews in rounds

Here is what I do with clients. It usually runs three to five sessions over a few weeks.

**Round one: the story.** I ask the founder how the business started, what went wrong early, and what they would tell themselves on day one. I am not after a biography. I am listening for the moments where a rule got formed. "After that client, I stopped doing fixed-price work." That sentence is a policy, and it came out as a story.

**Round two: the customer.** Who is the ideal client? Describe the last one you loved working with. Describe the last one you fired. What did they say in the first call that told you which kind they were? What are they afraid of when they hire someone like you? What do they always ask?

**Round three: the work.** Walk me through a project from first contact to final invoice. Where do you personally have to be involved? Where does it stall? What do you check before anything goes out the door?

**Round four: the voice.** Show me three pieces of writing that sound like you and three that make you wince. What words do you never use? How do you open an email to a new prospect? What is the thing you say in every sales conversation that you have never written down?

**Round five: the gaps.** By now the founder has read the organized notes from the first four rounds and has a list of "oh, and also." This round is almost always the richest.

I record every session and have it transcribed. Then I sort what came out into categories.

## The categories that matter

The organized output is the foundation layer of Brand Voice AI, and it looks like this:

- **Identity:** mission, values, origin, what you refuse to do
- **Audience:** avatars, fears, triggers, the questions they ask
- **Offers:** what you sell, how you describe it, what it includes and excludes
- **Process:** the steps, the checkpoints, the places a human must decide
- **Voice:** tone, vocabulary, structure, do's and don'ts, example pieces
- **Stories:** the anecdotes that teach a rule better than the rule does
- **Standards:** what must be true before anything is published, sent, or delivered

A founder's knowledge almost always lands in all seven. If a category comes up empty, that is a finding too. A business with no written standards is a business where quality depends on who is having a good day.

## The 674-file lesson

The reason I build it this way is that I did it to myself first.

In July 2026, I pulled 674 files out of a ChatGPT workspace I had been using for over three years. Marketing plans, drafts, research, half-built frameworks, conversation logs. I had been doing exactly what every founder does: having the thinking, then moving on without organizing it. The thinking was not lost, but it was useless, because it was scattered across hundreds of files with names like "Untitled 47."

Sorting those files into the seven categories above took weeks. Along the way I found rules I had forgotten I had, stories I had told dozens of times but never written down, and three versions of my own positioning that contradicted each other. By the end, I had something another person could read and understand, and something an AI tool could read and work from.

That sorting process became the interview method. Instead of waiting until a founder has 674 files of chaos, I go get the knowledge while it is still in their head and put it in order on the way out.

## The veteran who could not sell

The story I tell most often is about a fellow veteran who spent years building a service business and decided it was time to sell. He had revenue, repeat customers, and a reputation. Buyers looked at it and all said a version of the same thing: "You are the business."

Every process ran through him. Every customer relationship was his. Every decision about pricing, quality, and who to take on lived in his judgment, and his judgment was not written anywhere. A buyer would be paying for a company that stopped working the day he left.

He did not have a bad business. He had an undocumented one. The knowledge was real and valuable and completely trapped. Capturing it earlier would not have changed what he knew; it would have changed what he could sell.

Most founders will never sell. The problem still applies. Every hire you train, every assistant you hand work to, every AI tool you try to use is a buyer of your knowledge, and they are all getting the same answer that buyer got.

## What to do with it once it is out

Captured knowledge that sits in a document is only slightly better than knowledge in a head. The point is to use it:

- New hires read it in week one instead of absorbing it over a year
- Your assistant or contractor checks it before asking you
- AI tools are given it as context, so their drafts sound like your business instead of a generic one
- You read it yourself once a quarter and notice what has changed

That last one matters. Knowledge capture is not a one-time event. The second pass is always better than the first, and the business keeps learning.

## A simple first exercise

If you want to start tonight without a consultant, try this. Open a voice memo app and answer one question out loud for ten minutes: "What do I know about my customers that nobody else in my business knows?" Do not edit. Do not organize. Just talk.

Then get it transcribed and read it. You will find at least three rules you have never written down. That is the method, scaled down to one round.

If you would rather have someone run the full process with you, that is what a Brand Voice AI foundation session is. And if you are not sure how much of your business is trapped in your head, the Business Systems Assessment is a seven-minute gut check on exactly that question.

# AI Has a New Name in Washington. Laughable or Not, Learn It.

URL: https://poguedigitalsolutions.com/blog/ai-has-a-new-name-in-washington
Published: 2026-10-05  Updated: 2026-10-05  Topic: AI Industry and Policy

**The short answer:** Federal agencies now call AI "super intelligence," and a new Super Intelligence Force led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has 120 days to report on AI's risks and opportunities. The name change is mostly PR, but small business owners should learn the term, use both words for a while, and watch for the task force report around early February 2027.

Last week the President signed an executive order telling federal agencies to stop saying "artificial intelligence" and start saying "super intelligence." On Sunday he followed it up by announcing a new Super Intelligence Force.

My first reaction was simple. Here we go again. The Gulf of Mexico became the Gulf of America, and now AI gets a new name tag. It's a PR stunt.

I still think that. I also think small business owners can't afford to roll their eyes and move on, and I'll explain why.

## What actually happened

Here is the news without the spin.

- **The name change.** Federal agencies are directed to use "Super Intelligence" and "SI" instead of "AI" in official communications, as far as the law allows. The legal definition of AI stays the same for now. The White House science adviser has 60 days to propose a legal definition of "Super Intelligence."
- **The task force.** Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton chairs it, which makes him the new AI czar. The vice chairs are FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson, Undersecretary of War Emil Michael, and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor.
- **The assignment.** The group reportedly has 120 days to deliver a report on the risks and opportunities of AI. Its charter talks about planning for AI-enabled threats while avoiding overregulation that would slow innovation and competition.
- **The mindset.** Clayton has said one of the biggest risks is "not being first," and he opposes any pause in AI development.

## Why rename it at all?

The only thing a new name does right now is cause confusion. Same tools, same technology, two words for it.

So why bother? My read is that this is about removing the scary. For forty years "AI" has carried Hollywood baggage. Say it to most people over 40 and somebody brings up Skynet. "Super intelligence" sounds like a product upgrade. It sounds like something you want on your side.

I don't think the new term makes AI scarier. I think it was picked to do the opposite.

## Speed is good. Guardrails are better.

I understand the argument for speed. Nobody wants to fall behind China on the most important technology of our lifetime.

But there needs to be a balance. We are racing a country many believe let COVID slip out of a lab. If we're worried about what they build, the answer is better guardrails on both sides of the race, and a plan for what happens when something gets loose. What's next, infected AI?

Being first matters. Being first with no brakes is how you end up first to the crash.

## Leadership needs oversight

Look at who's running this task force: the intelligence chief, the FTC chair, a Pentagon official, and the head of the federal HR office. Those are serious people. None of them come from the small business world, and none of them build these tools.

The point of government is to govern. That means somebody has to lead, and I'm glad someone is in charge. Leadership is key, but always with oversight. A 120-day report written by a group whose chairman says the biggest risk is losing the race should get a hard look from Congress, from industry, and from the people who will live with the results.

That report should land around early February 2027. Put it on your calendar.

## I've built this translation table before

Years ago, Cox Communications merged its regional call centers into three large centers. Every region had its own names for things and its own way of doing them. Suddenly I was taking calls from all over, and customers and coworkers were using words that meant nothing in our area.

So I built a spreadsheet. One column for where the call came from, one for what they called it, one for what it meant to us.

Nobody had to love the new terms. We just had to understand each other so we could do the job.

That's where small business owners are right now. Washington has a new word for the tools you already use. Your clients will see it in the news, your vendors will start putting it in their marketing, and government forms and contracts will use it. If you don't know that SI means AI, you'll be the one confused in the meeting.

## What to do with this

1. **Learn the term.** Laughable or not, it's out there. Super intelligence, SI, and AI all point to the same tools, like Claude, that you may already be using.
2. **Build your own translation table.** If you write proposals, bid on government work, or explain AI to clients, use both terms for a while so nobody gets lost.
3. **Don't let the new name change your judgment.** A friendlier name doesn't make a tool safer. Keep checking what AI writes for you, protect your customers' data, and stay the human in charge.
4. **Watch for the February report.** That's where real rules, money, or mandates could show up.

Call it AI. Call it SI. Call it whatever you want. The work is the same, and so is the responsibility that comes with it.

What do you think? Smart move, PR stunt, or both?

*John M Pogue is the founder of Pogue Digital Solutions, LLC, helping small businesses put AI to work in their own voice.*

## Further reading

# Why I Named My AI Assistant Ms MoneyPenny

URL: https://poguedigitalsolutions.com/blog/why-i-named-my-ai-assistant-ms-moneypenny
Published: 2026-09-26  Updated: 2026-09-26  Topic: AI and Automation

My ex-wife worked as a land tech. In the oil and gas business, that means she was the executive assistant to a landman, the person who tracks down mineral owners and negotiates the leases. On paper, her job was paperwork. In practice, she ran his world.

Talking with her, I learned what that job took. She kept him organized and on time. She took his scattered thoughts, his half-finished plans, his hopes for the next deal, and his meetings, and turned them into a day he could get through. She knew which calls he wanted and which ones he was dodging. She understood his heart well enough to answer for him when he wasn't in the room, and she knew when to say, "Let me check with him first."

She was the gatekeeper. She was the confidant. And nothing got done without her help.

That's the job I wanted filled when I started building an AI assistant. So I named her after the most famous executive assistant in fiction: Miss Moneypenny, who sits outside M's office in the James Bond films. Everybody has to get past her desk. She knows everything going on at MI6; she keeps the agents in line, and the boss trusts her completely.

I gave mine a small update. She's my Ms MoneyPenny, and she works for Pogue Digital Solutions, LLC and Brand Voice AI.

Her rules come straight from what I learned talking with my ex-wife in that landman's office. She reads everything and drafts everything, but nothing goes out without my yes. When something needs my judgment, she brings me what happened, what she checked, and what she recommends, then lets me decide. She keeps me organized and on time, and she guards my calendar like it matters, because it does.

I run two businesses, write 4 books, and work on one screenplay, and my thoughts, plans, and meetings scatter across both of them. Ms MoneyPenny pulls them back together. Like the land tech who taught me what the job means, she knows that nothing gets done without her help.

Want one of your own? Let's get on a discovery call. We'll find the "hot mess" in your business that needs organizing, and I'll build an assistant that sorts it out for you. Take your time back!

Send me a DM with the word MONEYPENNY, and I'll get you on my calendar.

# A Starship Traded Its Library for a Ride Home

URL: https://poguedigitalsolutions.com/blog/a-starship-traded-its-library-for-a-ride-home
Published: 2026-09-24  Updated: 2026-09-24  Topic: Brand Voice

*What a 1995 Star Trek episode says about standing out when AI can post a thousand times a day*

I spent this week at Funnel Hacking Live, the ClickFunnels conference, where this year's theme was "The A.I. Era." One idea kept coming back from the stage: AI can now produce social media faster than any person or team. Peter Swain, an AI educator who works with service businesses, described a man who was publishing 20 posts a day. His goal was 1,000. That is one post every 86 seconds, around the clock. The algorithms are letting it all through.

So here is the question I wrote in my notes. If one person can publish 1,000 posts a day, how does anyone find yours? People scrolling will have a harder time finding anything original.

AI can draft all day, but it can't decide what matters to your client, what to leave out, or when to say nothing. Your stories are what truly set you apart, making you feel valued and confident in your authenticity.

A Star Trek episode from 1995 made that case better than I can.

## The planet that paid for stories

In the first season of *Star Trek: Voyager*, the ship is stranded 70,000 light-years from Earth. At full speed, the trip home would take about 75 years. Each episode, the crew looks for a faster way.

In "Prime Factors," they find one. They meet the Sikarians, a warm, pleasure-loving people whose culture treats stories as a measure of a person's character. A good story is a gift. A new story is treasure. In one moment I still remember, a crew member tells a small, funny story about two people on the ship, and the Sikarian listening asks for permission to retell it. That is how seriously they held ownership of a story.

The Sikarians also had a device called a spatial trajector. It could fold space and move a person 40,000 light-years in a single jump. For Voyager, that was more than half the distance home.

Captain Janeway offered a trade: the ship's entire library of literature for the trajector. The Sikarian leader said no. Their law forbade sharing their technology.

Then a Sikarian named Jaret Otel came forward with a quiet offer. He would hand over the trajector in exchange for the library. He wanted to be the one who brought all those new stories to his people, and the prestige that came with it.

Janeway refused. She would not go around another people's laws to get her crew home, even though she wanted to get them home more than anything.

Some of her crew saw it differently. Tuvok, her most trusted officer, made the trade behind her back. B'Elanna Torres and two engineers tried to install the device. They were being human about it. Yes, it broke the rules. It would also get everyone home to their families.

It failed. The trajector only worked on the Sikarian homeworld because it drew power from the planet's crystal mantle. When they switched it on, it nearly blew up the ship. Torres destroyed it with a phaser.

## Why this story stays with me

A civilization that could jump a person 40,000 light-years valued stories more than that technology. One of them was willing to break his own laws to get them first.

Think about what that says about scarcity. The Sikarians had the machine. What they didn't have were the stories of a crew from the other side of the galaxy: their families, their mistakes, the small funny moments between two people on a ship.

That is where we are with AI. The machine is everywhere now. Anyone can generate 1,000 posts a day. No tool can generate the day you had, the patient you held a hand for, the customer who called back to say thank you, or the thing your son said at dinner. Those belong to you.

The episode has a second lesson, and I think it matters just as much. The crew grabbed a shortcut that only worked under someone else's conditions. Once they left that planet, it fell apart and nearly took the ship with it. A thousand AI posts a day works on the algorithm's terms, until the algorithm changes. Your stories go wherever you go.

## How to put your stories to work

**Keep a story log.** When something happens that makes you laugh, teaches you something, or changes your mind, write down three lines about it that day. You will forget the details faster than you think.

**Give credit, and ask when it's personal.** If a story or idea came from someone else, say where you got it. Respecting others' stories builds trust and makes your audience feel valued.

**You don't need a dramatic turning point.** The Sikarians valued a short, funny story about two crewmates. Small, specific moments make your stories relatable and meaningful to others.

**Let AI assist in shaping your story:** tightening drafts or finding stronger openings, while ensuring the core memory, feeling, and point remain authentically yours.

## The trade I'd make

Janeway knew what her crew's stories were worth. She was willing to trade the whole library to get them home, and she still would not cheat to do it.

Your stories are worth that much too. In a feed filling up at one post every 86 seconds, they are the one thing nobody else can produce. Tell them, protect them, and give credit when they belong to someone else.

The Sikarians would have paid for yours.

*John M Pogue: Curiosity is my superpower.*

## References

- "Prime Factors (Star Trek: Voyager)." Wikipedia. [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Factors_(Star_Trek:_Voyager)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Factors_(Star_Trek:_Voyager))
- "Prime Factors (episode)." Memory Alpha. [https://memory-alpha.fandom.com/wiki/Prime_Factors_(episode)](https://memory-alpha.fandom.com/wiki/Prime_Factors_(episode))

- Keith R.A. DeCandido, "Star Trek: Voyager Rewatch: 'Prime Factors.'" Reactor. [https://reactormag.com/star-trek-voyager-rewatch-prime-factors/](https://reactormag.com/star-trek-voyager-rewatch-prime-factors/)

# The Builders Asked for Brakes. The Government Gave Three Answers.

URL: https://poguedigitalsolutions.com/blog/the-builders-asked-for-brakes
Published: 2026-09-21  Updated: 2026-09-21  Topic: AI Industry and Policy

Before anyone closes a patient, the room counts.

Two people count sponges, needles, and instruments aloud against a written record. If the count comes up short, nobody closes. The surgeon does not close. The attending does not close. The case stops, the room goes quiet in a particular way, and everybody starts looking, because a sponge that is not on the table is somewhere worse.

I learned this as a Navy Hospital Corpsman, working in surgery. And the thing that struck me then, the thing I have carried into every job since, is who gets to call it.

The scrub tech and the circulating nurse, not the surgeon. The lowest-ranking people in the room hold the authority to stop the highest-ranking person in the room, and the reason is not fairness. The reason is line of sight. The surgeon is inside the patient. The scrub tech is looking at the table. Whoever can see the problem first gets the power to halt, or the power is useless.

That is the whole design, and it has nothing to do with courtesy. Risk shows up in one person's field of view before it shows up in anyone else's, so the system gets built around that person or it is theater.

I thought about the count all week.

## The industry called it one.

On the weekend of September 12, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay arguing that the companies building frontier AI should slow down together. He called it pacing the frontier. His proposals were specific: bring in independent evaluators who can look at safety, establish common safety standards across companies, and verify that anyone claiming to follow them actually does.

Sam Altman agreed publicly and said OpenAI would bring in independent evaluators too. OpenAI also delayed its expected public listing, which should get your attention, because delaying an IPO is not a press release. It costs money.

Elon Musk, Satya Nadella, and Demis Hassabis all broadly agreed over the same weekend, without committing to anything in particular.

And in the reporting around all of it, an Anthropic researcher named Evan Hubinger said he personally puts the odds that AI kills every human being on earth within the next decade at better than one in ten.

Read that sentence again and notice where it came from. That is a man describing the product he goes to work on.

The scrub tech called a count.

## The following Saturday

On September 19, President Trump posted on Truth Social that he is creating an AI Force, modeled on the Space Force he stood up in his first term, and that he will name an AI czar shortly.

The post said the government "will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry." He said bad behavior would be handled through, in his words, "our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System." He called the worry that AI could destroy humanity a hoax. He said the only guardrail the situation requires is a strong and smart president.

He also said AI could become the next Industrial Revolution and could account for as much as 25% of the country's GDP.

Put a number on that, because nobody else did. The American economy runs around 29 trillion dollars. Twenty-five percent of it is roughly 7.25 trillion. Every dollar this country spends on health care (every hospital stay, every prescription, every premium) added up to 5.3 trillion in 2024, which was 18% of GDP and made it the largest thing we buy. Manufacturing came in at 9.4% at the start of this year. So the claim on the table is that a single technology ends up worth more than American health care. That could happen. It has never happened; he posted it on social media, and no one was in a position to ask him to show his work.

The count got called. The answer from the top of the building was to keep cutting.

## Except that is not the whole government

Here is where it gets strange, and where I think most of the coverage is flattening something worth seeing.

While the White House was announcing a new force whose stated job is to protect the industry from interference, Congress was moving in the opposite direction. Dozens of AI bills have now been filed. Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Greg Casar introduced legislation to ban artificial superintelligence outright and temporarily pause advanced AI development. States are also being actively pushed out of the room. An executive order signed in December 2025, titled Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence, stood up a Justice Department task force to challenge state AI laws in federal court, directed the Commerce Department to identify state rules it considers overly burdensome, and conditioned 42 billion dollars in broadband funding on states declining to enforce certain AI regulations. That is not a government sitting this one out. That is a government using real leverage to ensure oversight happens.

The industry leaders and researchers developing AI, referred to as "the builders," asked for brakes, and the government produced three answers at once. Ban it. Regulate it. Clear the field and handle the wreckage in court afterward.

Handling harm through the existing criminal and civil justice system means you find out afterward. It means the sponge is already inside the patient and now we are in litigation about whose sponge it was.

An AI Force is a real thing to announce. A czar is a real position to fill. But announcing an oversight body whose declared purpose is to prevent oversight is a sentence I had to read four times.

## We have run this play twice before

None of this is new. It is the third time an American industry has stood at this exact fork, and the first two went the other direction.

In 1968, Jack Valenti built the film rating system, with four categories: G, M, R, and X. The Motion Picture Association's own history says he created it "amid mounting calls for censorship and the specter of government intervention." Local censorship boards were cutting films city by city, and Washington was circling. Valenti's answer was to rate the movies before somebody else did it for him.

In December 1993, the Senate held hearings on violent video games, driven by Mortal Kombat, Night Trap, and Doom. Senators Joe Lieberman and Herb Kohl ran them, and Kohl put the choice in one sentence: "If you don't do something about [content ratings], we will."

The industry moved fast. It announced a ratings system hours before the December 9 hearing even opened. Seven companies formed a trade association by April. The Entertainment Software Rating Board went live on September 13, 1994, nine months after Kohl said that out loud.

Look at the shape of both. The government said Regulate yourselves or we will, and the industry, facing a credible threat, built a rating body in months.

Now reverse every arrow. In September 2026, the companies building the most powerful technology on earth asked, publicly and in writing, to be evaluated by outsiders and held to a common standard. The branch of government that would have to enforce any of it replied that it "will not in any way hinder or stifle" them.

Valenti had to be pushed. Amodei volunteered. Volunteering turns out to be worth less.

## Both of those worked because somebody refused to carry the product

A rating is a piece of paper, and paper does not stop anything. What stopped things was the shelf.

Take Basic Instinct in 1992. The ratings board looked at what Paul Verhoeven turned in and gave it an NC-17. He went back eight times and cut roughly forty seconds to get it changed to an R, and those same seconds were restored for the director's cut that premiered at Cannes that May. Nobody was arrested, and no law was broken. An NC-17 in 1992 meant theater chains wouldn't book the picture and newspapers wouldn't run the ad, so three letters from a private board cost a studio its distribution. When the longer version reached home video, it came out as an unrated director's cut, which tells you the studio feared the letters, not the footage.

In 2005, someone found that Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas had shipped with a sexual minigame sitting in the code, disabled but present on the disc. The mod that surfaced it was called Hot Coffee. And the voluntary system that most people assumed was decorative did something nobody expected.

The ESRB revoked the game's M rating and re-rated it Adults Only. Retailers pulled it off the shelves. Take-Two suspended production and recalled it. The company shipped a patch, stripped the code, and reissued the game as an M. The FTC settled with Take-Two and Rockstar in June 2006 over advertising a rating the disc did not match.

That is the whole machine working. A private body re-rated a product, the product came off the shelf, and the company ate the cost. No legislation passed, and none had to.

## Which is the condition AI does not have

The count in an operating room works for three reasons. Everyone counts the same items the same way. Somebody outside the room checks the record. And when the stop gets called, the case actually stops.

Amodei proposed the first two. Independent evaluators are the outside check, common safety standards are the shared count, and to his credit, he put both in writing.

The third one is the problem, and the two rating systems are exactly why.

Film and games each had a chokepoint. Between the studio and the audience stood a theater chain. Between the publisher and the kid stood Walmart, Target, and GameStop. When a rating changed, those companies refused to carry the product, and that refusal was the enforcement. The rating boards never needed police power because retail already had it.

A frontier model has no shelf. It ships from the company that built it, over an API, to anyone with a credit card, in every country at once. No exhibitor can decline the booking, and no buyer at Target can pull the pallet. Take the chokepoint out of the ESRB, and what you have left is a logo.

So a lab can slow down, a competitor can decline to, and nothing anywhere in the distribution path punishes the second lab. That is the structure, not a moral failure on anyone's part. Self-regulation without an enforced stop is a promise, and promises are worth exactly as much as the cost of breaking them.

## The case against the people I just made sound noble

A company asking to be regulated is not automatically acting against its own interest. Independent evaluations, compliance verification, and common safety standards are expensive. Expensive rules are survivable for a lab with billions in backing and fatal for a startup with eleven people. Amodei may be entirely sincere and the proposal may still, as a side effect, pull the ladder up. Both are possible at once, and neither cancels the other.

There is also a straight-faced argument for the White House position that deserves better than a sneer. If American labs pace themselves and Chinese labs do not, the pacing did not reduce the risk; it relocated it. A unilateral slowdown in a race with more than one runner is a transfer, not a brake. You cannot wave that away, and the people who do are usually the ones who have never had to hold a position against a competitor who does not share it.

What I will not extend the same patience to is the word hoax. You can argue that the risk is overstated. You can argue the timelines are wrong. Calling it a hoax means claiming the people raising it are lying, and the people raising it this month are the CEOs of the companies building it, plus their own researchers, several of whom are putting numbers on the odds. Somebody in that picture is wrong. Nobody in that picture appears to be running a con.

## What I would actually do with this

If you run something small, this week changed nothing about your Monday, and I am not going to pretend otherwise. But it changed what you should expect, and there are four things I would do.

Assume the rules arrive late and arrive unevenly. With the White House leaning one way, Congress leaning another, and the states fighting for the right to act at all, you won't get one clear rule you can build against. Write down now which AI systems touch your customers, what data goes into them, and who at your company signed off. You are building that record for a question somebody asks you in 2028.

Find out who in your building can stop the work. Whatever tool you have running, someone has line of sight on it that you do not. Whoever that person is, they need standing authority to halt it without asking permission, and they need to know they have it. A stop that requires escalation is not a stop.

Expect the rule that binds you to come from a company, not from Congress. That is the lesson of both rating systems. What disciplined the studios was a theater chain declining to book the picture. What disciplined Rockstar was Walmart clearing the shelf. If you build on somebody's AI, your real regulator is your vendor's terms of service, your app store's review policy, and your payment processor. Read those the way you would read a statute, because they will change faster than one.

Watch what companies spend, not what they say. OpenAI delayed a public offering. That is the most informative fact in this entire story, because everything else cost nothing to say. Apply that filter to every AI vendor pitching you this quarter. Statements are free.

Last thing.

The count is not really about sponges. Any competent surgeon knows roughly what went in. The count exists because the room agreed, in advance and in writing, on who gets to say stop, and it agreed while everyone was calm and nobody was bleeding.

That agreement is the product. The counting is just the part you can see.

Right now, the people closest to this technology are telling us the count is off. Congress wants to ban the procedure. The states are arguing about whether they are even allowed in the room. And the White House has announced that it is standing up a new force whose job, as described, is to make sure nobody stops the surgery.

We are going to settle who holds the authority to call a halt. The only question left is whether we settle it before or after somebody closes.

*John M Pogue writes about how systems fail the people inside them. Curiosity is my superpower*

## Further reading

For anyone who wants to follow a thread beyond what this piece covers.

**On whether self-regulation forecloses regulation.** [Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association, 564 U.S. 786 (2011)](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/564/786/). The Supreme Court struck down California's law restricting violent video game sales to minors on First Amendment grounds. A working voluntary rating system is part of the backdrop. It is the strongest argument that rating yourself well enough can permanently take the legislative option off the table.

**On the chokepoint, and how the industry routed around it.** [In the pic-to-DVD shift, 'unrated' rates high](https://variety.com/2004/digital/features/in-pic-to-dvd-shift-unrated-rates-high-1117910285), Variety, 2004. Studios learned to ship unrated home video rather than carry the NC-17 letters, and when both versions sat on a shelf together, the unrated one took 80 to 90 percent of sales. Worth reading alongside the claim that retail enforcement held.

# AI's "Wild West" Phase Needs a Regulator, Not a Waiver

URL: https://poguedigitalsolutions.com/blog/ais-wild-west-phase-needs-a-regulator-not-a-waiver
Published: 2026-09-15  Updated: 2026-09-15  Topic: AI Industry and Policy

Last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay arguing the AI industry needs to slow down. Within hours, OpenAI's Sam Altman agreed. Both said the same thing in almost the same words: AI companies need to coordinate on safety standards before capability outruns control.

To actually do that legally, they're asking the U.S. government for an antitrust waiver. That's the detail that should stop you.

Antitrust law exists for exactly one reason: to stop competitors from getting in a room together and deciding the rules for everyone else. That's not a technicality. That's the whole point of the law. When the two most powerful AI labs in the world ask for permission to have that conversation anyway, they're telling you, out loud, that what they want to do would normally be illegal.

Maybe it should be illegal. Let me tell you why I think there's a better way.

## I spent years inside one of the most regulated industries in the country: debt collection.

Before the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, it was the Wild West. I heard the stories, collectors calling people pretending to be from a law office, working the fear until the debt got paid, whatever else it took. Some of it was flatly illegal even then. A lot of it lived in the gray area, and gray areas get pushed until someone draws a line.

Once the regulation landed, the industry didn't become perfect. It never does. But every company had the same rulebook. Nobody could out-compete an honest business by being willing to lie harder. The line got drawn once, publicly, by someone with no stake in who won.

## That's what AI is missing right now.

Every AI company is in the same trap collectors were in before regulation: pushing into gray areas not because they think it's right, but because if they don't, a competitor will, and they'll fall behind. Amodei's essay is basically an admission of that trap. His fix, get permission to coordinate privately, just moves the trap somewhere with less sunlight.

We've solved this exact shape of problem before, in a different industry too. After Enron, nobody trusted that a public company's own hand-picked, self-paid auditor would tell the truth about its books. So Sarbanes-Oxley created an independent board to oversee auditors instead of leaving companies to pay their own referees. It worked because the people checking the work didn't answer to the people being checked.

## Here's what I'd build instead of a waiver: a federal agency modeled on that same fix.

Call it the Federal AI Practices Bureau. It sets the safety standards Amodei is asking labs to agree on privately, except publicly, where anyone can see how the standards got set. It hires the third-party evaluators, the METRs of the world, and puts those contracts out to competitive bid, the same way any government contract works. The AI companies pay into it, the same way regulated industries fund their own oversight today. Nobody's paying their own grader anymore, and nobody needs an antitrust exemption to talk to a competitor, because they're not setting the rules together. A regulator is setting them for everyone.

Is this slower than an essay and a handshake? Yes. Building a real agency takes time, and AI capability isn't waiting around for Congress. And a domestic bureau has no authority over what gets built in Beijing. That piece runs through the State Department, not the FAIPB. But diplomacy with a rival government isn't a light switch. The closest working model we have for getting a rival nation to accept outside verification on dangerous technology is something like the International Atomic Energy Agency: decades of negotiation and inspections, and still imperfect compliance from the countries most determined to cheat.

This isn't hypothetical. The 2025 CIA assessment on COVID's origin leans toward an accidental lab leak, at low confidence, in part because nobody outside that lab had the access to know for certain either way. That's what happens when research runs without independent eyes on it. Whatever actually happened in Wuhan, the lesson holds for AI: a lab with no outside verification is a lab where accidents don't get caught until it's too late to matter.

State Department involvement opens that track. It doesn't finish it overnight, and nobody should pretend otherwise.

But a slow, public referee beats a fast, private cartel every time. We've done this twice already: once for the people collecting your debt, once for the people auditing your public companies. It's time to do it a third time, before the gray areas become the whole map.

## References and Further Reading

# Siri AI Ships Monday.

URL: https://poguedigitalsolutions.com/blog/siri-ai-ships-monday-apple-has-run-this-play-before
Published: 2026-09-09  Updated: 2026-09-09  Topic: AI Industry and Policy

*Apple Has Run This Play Before. Ask Motorola.*

On Monday, iOS 27 arrives, and Siri finally becomes something close to the assistant Apple promised us two years ago. Part of that new intelligence comes from Google, which agreed to be completely invisible inside the product. Apple pays roughly a billion dollars a year for access to the technology behind Gemini, and Google gets no logo, no branding, no relationship with the customer, on paper that looks like the partnership of the decade. I read it as a lease with a very carefully written exit clause.

Look at how we got here. In February 2024, Apple killed Project Titan, its self-driving car, after ten years and more than ten billion dollars. There was no press release, just an internal announcement. About two thousand people were on that team. The software and machine-learning folks moved into Apple's AI group. Roughly six hundred others, the battery engineers and the test drivers, got layoff notices. Four months later, Apple Intelligence was announced at WWDC, and the story became a decade of car research redirected into AI, all that talent pointed at something better. I spent ten years at Cox Communications, so I know that language. You'd ask where Cindy went because you hadn't seen her all week, and management would tell you she got promoted to customer. Redirected is a word that only ever describes the people still in the building. Then the rollout came late and thin. The personal-context Siri that got the loudest applause never shipped. By March 2025, Siri had been taken from the executive who owned it and handed to the Vision Pro lead. That July, the man running Apple's foundation models team left for Meta on a package reported at over $200 million, and at least three more of his researchers followed him out within the month. In November 2025, Bloomberg reported Apple was shopping for outside help. In January, Google signed the deal. Two and a half years from "we've got this" to "we need to buy this."

What shipped in June was not one Google model but a family of five. Four are Apple's own, trained on Apple's infrastructure and then refined using Gemini's output. Only the top tier is built on the licensed Google foundation, and only that tier runs on Google's cloud. The contract term that should make Google's board sit up straight is the right to distill. Apple paid Google to teach models that Apple owns outright and gets to keep running long after the contract ends. Apple's own AI server chip goes into mass production this year, and Apple-operated data centers are penciled in for 2027.

If that pattern feels familiar, it should. In 2004 Apple partnered with Motorola to put iTunes on a phone, and Motorola's CEO was thrilled. The ROKR launched at an Apple event in September 2005, crippled at exactly one hundred songs, on a carrier deal Apple didn't control. At that same event, Apple introduced the iPod nano and buried its own partner's launch in the coverage. The press called the ROKR the "CROCKR." Sixteen months later, Apple announced the iPhone on Cingular, the same carrier it had just spent two years learning how to negotiate with. Cingular was rebranding as AT&T that same year, which is why we all remember it as the AT&T exclusive. Motorola got a punchline. Apple got an education, and that failure is exactly what convinced Steve Jobs to build the phone himself.

Google is not Motorola, and I'll say so plainly. Motorola never saw it coming. Google runs a frontier lab, knows this playbook cold, and signed anyway, partly to keep OpenAI from owning the assistant layer on a billion iPhones. Google also pays Apple around twenty billion a year for search placement, so Apple can't discard it the way it discarded a handset maker, and federal judges are watching this one. Google priced the risk with its eyes open.

Strip the differences away and the shape is the same one Imagination Technologies saw when it lost Apple's GPU business overnight, and the one Intel saw when it lost the Mac and then sold Apple its modem division. Apple rarely walks in the front door of a new category. It walks in through somebody else's, next to a partner who already knows the room, and it pays close attention on the way in. Motorola knew phones and carriers. Intel knew silicon. Google knows frontier AI. Apple borrows the experience, keeps the customer, keeps the brand, and starts building the replacement in the room next door.

That's patience, and patience is rare. But if you run a small business and a giant ever offers to partner with you, ask what they're learning from you and what you get to keep once they've learned it. When only one side walks away smarter, that's an apprenticeship, not a partnership, and you're the teacher.

## References

Primary sources first, because most of what circulates on this deal is aggregator blogs recycling the same paragraph.

The five-model family, parameter counts, and Apple's own description of where Google's work touches it. <https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/introducing-third-generation-of-apple-foundation-models>

**The release date:** Apple confirms iOS 27 release date: September 14 (9to5Mac) <https://9to5mac.com/2026/09/09/apple-confirms-ios-27-release-date-september-14/>

**The talent Apple lost first:** Meta Poached Apple's Ruoming Pang With Pay Package Over $200 Million (Bloomberg, paywalled) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2025-07-09/meta-poached-apple-s-pang-with-pay-package-over-200-million>

Apple Continues Losing AI Experts to Meta (MacRumors) <https://www.macrumors.com/2025/07/29/apple-continues-losing-ai-experts-to-meta/>

Confirms the 100-song cap, the iPod nano launching the same day, and that Cingular became AT&T in 2007. <https://www.gsmarena.com/flashback_the_motorola_rokr_e1_was_a_dud_but_it_paved_the_way_for_the_iphone-news-38934.php>

## Further reading

**If you only read one thing beyond Apple's own paper,** Apple's Gemini-Siri Deal Is the Next Microsoft Antitrust Case, Not the Next App Store Fight (Luis Blanquez, The Antitrust Attorney Blog, May 2026). The sharpest argument published on this deal: Apple does not compete with Gemini; it neutralizes it by absorbing it, and swapping suppliers does not cure a foreclosure problem. <https://www.theantitrustattorney.com/apples-gemini-siri-deal-is-the-next-microsoft-antitrust-case-not-the-next-app-store-fight/>

**The counterargument, worth reading against the grain:** Apple's new foundation models don't contain a drop of Gemini (AppleInsider). The headline overcorrects, and the comments do a good job explaining why.
